title: Post-incident hardening checklist
body_md:
## Close the route the attacker used—and test recovery

After urgent containment, turn the incident timeline into a prioritized repair list. Do not rotate every password merely because one account sent a phishing message; identify credentials that were shared, reused, stored on a controlled device, or reachable through the compromised mailbox. Change those through known-good devices and official account pages. A password manager can generate unique replacements, but if its own account or device was exposed, secure that access first.

### Account and recovery paths

Review active sessions and sign them out where the provider allows. Check recovery email, phone, backup codes, mail forwarding, filters, connected apps and app-specific passwords. Removing a visible forwarding rule is not enough if another authorized app or recovery address still gives access. Choose the strongest practical sign-in the service offers; WebAuthn/FIDO2 passkeys or security keys resist phishing better than manually entered codes, but availability and account recovery differ. SMS may still be the only offered method; use it rather than no second factor while securing the carrier account. Store backup options so losing one device does not lock you out.

### Device and money paths

Install supported security updates on devices used in the incident. Remove unrecognized remote-support software and browser extensions after documenting what happened. Run reputable security tools or seek manufacturer/organizational help for suspected malware. A clean scan is reassuring but not proof; a managed work device follows the employer's procedure. If a card number was exposed, follow the issuer's replacement and monitoring instructions; an account transfer problem may require different controls. Check statements and alerts over time. A US credit freeze or Russian loan self-ban addresses only its defined new-credit scope.

### A short follow-up checklist

- Confirm affected passwords are unique and recovery contacts are yours.
- Review sessions, forwarding and connected apps again after several days.
- Ask your carrier about number-transfer protection if the number was involved.
- Enable bank transaction alerts and track the open dispute or replacement card.
- Schedule a later review of the incident record with a trusted person or workplace team when appropriate.

### Define “done” with evidence

Make a short table: exposure, control changed, confirmation, owner, follow-up date. Recheck a few days later that recovery contacts and forwarding have stayed correct; follow the bank/provider case until it has an outcome. Closure is a decision based on known risks, not certainty that every unseen attacker action is discovered. Keep a way to reopen the case if a delayed alert or fraudulent account appears.

widget_config.goal: Turn the incident's entry path into a verifiable repair and follow-up checklist, with limits for each control.
widget_config.today_action: Check the recovery email/phone and active sessions of one important account through its official settings; record any change in a private checklist.
widget_config.scope: General consumer hardening; authenticator choices, device support, banking controls and credit measures vary by provider and jurisdiction.

blocks.title: The password changed, but access remains
blocks.situation: Synthetic: after an email takeover, Nika changes the password. A week later, a hidden forwarding rule still sends copies outside her mailbox.
blocks.analysis: The password change addressed one path but not the persistence mechanism. She removes the rule, checks connected apps/recovery contacts and sessions, then verifies settings again later.

blocks.title: An expected connected app
blocks.situation: Synthetic: a calendar app appears in Luis's account permissions. He installed it and confirms its exact permissions through the provider's settings.
blocks.analysis: An unfamiliar-looking name is not automatically malicious. He can keep a needed app with understood permissions and remove any stale grants; indiscriminate revocation could disrupt work.

blocks.title: Find the remaining route
blocks.setup: Synthetic: a mailbox was used to send fake invoices. The password has been changed, but the incident review is not finished.

choices.text: Forwarding rules, recovery contacts, sessions and connected apps.
choices.consequence: You look for remaining access paths.
choices.explanation: Changing the password alone may leave delegated access.

choices.consequence: It does not explain account persistence.

steps.prompt: A known calendar app is listed. What do you do?

choices.text: Verify owner and permissions, then keep or revoke based on actual need.
choices.consequence: Legitimate access stays usable and excess access is reduced.
choices.explanation: Do not label a connected app malicious solely by name.

choices.text: Report the app as proof of the attacker.
choices.consequence: You may misclassify a normal tool.

steps.prompt: You suspect the laptop had remote-support software. How do you change credentials?

choices.text: Use a trusted device, remove the software with reputable help, then review affected credentials.
choices.consequence: New passwords are less likely to be observed.

choices.text: Change them on the same uncontrolled laptop.
choices.consequence: The new secrets might be captured.
choices.explanation: A password change on a watched device can fail.

steps.prompt: What makes the review complete enough to close?

choices.text: Document controls, confirmation and follow-up dates; reopen if new evidence appears.
choices.consequence: The decision is traceable and revisable.
choices.explanation: No checklist can prove an attacker did nothing unseen.

choices.text: Declare permanent safety because one scan is clean.
choices.consequence: Unknown paths or delayed fraud remain possible.
choices.explanation: A scan is not a guarantee.

blocks.debrief: Repair the specific route, check adjacent recovery paths and verify the result later. Retry choices and replay; a completed checklist is a reasoned snapshot, not a promise.

questions.prompt: A password is changed but a stranger's recovery email remains. Is the account secured?

choices.text: Yes; password changes remove all other access.
choices.explanation: The recovery address can restore access.

choices.text: No; remove the unauthorized recovery path and review sessions.
choices.explanation: Both credential and recovery routes matter.

questions.prompt: A service offers SMS MFA only. What is the practical choice?

choices.text: Use SMS as offered and protect the carrier account while watching for stronger options.
choices.explanation: A second factor can still help, though SMS has SIM-swap risk.

choices.text: Disable MFA until a security key is supported.

questions.prompt: A clean malware scan proves the device was never controlled. True?

choices.explanation: Scans have limits and cannot establish complete history.

choices.text: False; use the scan as one signal and seek trusted help when needed.
choices.explanation: The response depends on exposure and device ownership.
